children: The European Union wants to give national and local authorities legal clarity to curb short-term property rentals, as cities popular with tourists look for ways to contain rising housing costs.
EU competition commissioner Teresa Ribera said in a statement on Wednesday that the 27-member bloc faces a "terrible crisis" preventing many citizens from accessing housing.

While the so-called Affordable Housing Act doesn't restrict short-term rentals itself, the European Commission--the bloc's executive arm--wants to set up a framework that regional authorities can use to assess areas that are under "housing stress" due to tourist rentals before they take proportionate measures.

Europeans have struggled with rising house prices across the bloc for years, which some residents in tourist hotspots attribute to the proliferation of homes listed on platforms such as Airbnb in their cities.
Some bodies have already taken action. In Barcelona, a city that drew some 16 million visitors last year, the municipal government has moved to eliminate short-term rentals by 2028.
"With the Affordable Housing Act, we are providing legal certainty to local authorities, enabling them to take action and address one of the biggest problems of our time," Ribera said.
Other cities such as Florence and Madrid have also taken actions of their own, though some moves by regional governments have led to court spats with rental providers.

The commission said that authorities would need to show that short-term rentals have had a significant adverse impact on housing in their areas for three years. The act establishes a way to screen home affordability relative to incomes in a particular region before looking at other areas such as demand and supply and local demographics, while local governments can also use more granular data.

It also comes alongside a recommendation to nudge cities into increasing the supply of affordable homes by preparing so-called housing acceleration plans, touching areas like faster permitting and building conversion.

The plan has faced some industry criticism. Tech trade group CCIA Europe, which counts Airbnb as a member, said on Wednesday that there is still a risk that disproportionate restrictions could be imposed unchallenged. Lobby group EU Travel Tech--whose members include Airbnb as well as Booking.com and Expedia--called the move "misguided and not grounded on facts and data."
However, Ribera told reporters on Wednesday that many authorities have already taken action and the commission has been listening to their concerns.
"In some of Europe's most popular tourist destinations and city centers, short term rentals can account for up to 20% of homes," she said, adding that impacts pricing and stock.
